utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, your next witness, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The next witness is Sabit Kadriu. Before the witness comes in, there's one matter that I'd just like to address briefly. We will be requesting, as we've indicated in our witness notification, that the witness be transformed from a live witness to a combined live and combined 92 ter witness. And we would be asking for the admission of the witness's statement signed on the 10th of December, 2000. In agreement with Norman Sepenuk, we will not be seeking to have one particular paragraph admitted. It is on paragraph -- on page, sorry, 11. The paragraph about the middle of the page which begins: "It was a September offensive that made me believe that ..." that paragraph we will not seek to have admitted as part of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You may be re-assured to know that I wrote in brackets "we are not going down this road."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Whether I am re-assured, I'm not sure, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is one thing I overlooked before starting. I see that Mr. Milutinovic is absent, and I was alerted to this. Mr. O'Sullivan, I take it there isn't any problem associated with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: You're correct, Your Honour ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. There is one other matter that I would like to be clear about before we start, Mr. Marcussen. The latter part of the statement is largely compiled of lists. Now, the first list of 104 I can place in the indictment. Can you help me with what follows from page 24?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Those are a number of incidents which are not scheduled in the indictment. We would seek these parts admitted as context evidence for the events in Vushtrri, and for that purpose only -- like we had some of this evidence come in when witness -- Dr. Gerxhaliu was here. He also spoke about some of these incidents. The only thing I intended to do today is get one point of clarification about the 22 May incident that I understand the witness has been involved in investigating and has information about what happened to the missing persons and that will tie in to some forensic evidence that will come later. But I was not intending to spend much time on this part of the statement today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, but the statement is likely to be admitted, as you know, and we have to make what we can of it. But you've confirmed what I thought, that it could be no more than background context or the specific allegations to which the statement does relate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Indeed. It ties in with the issue of whether or not there was a campaign and whether or not there was -- there's a bigger picture which also -- well, on the national level -- eventually on the Kosovo level, there would be discussions about the nature of the campaign that took place there, but also on a smaller scale in the Vushtrri municipality. But as I said, you're absolutely right, it's not -- they're not scheduled incidents. We're not attempting to get the evidence in for any crime-base purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, the witness can now be brought into court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Maybe I should respect the custom of just indicating the paragraphs in the indictment. It's paragraph 25 and 26 -- and 26 -- 72(m), 75(i), 77(d), paragraph 88, paragraph 90, 94, 95, and 96, and then Schedule I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kadriu.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration by reading aloud the document now placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Kadriu, this -- the Court has before it a lengthy statement of your evidence, which we've read, so we are aware of the evidence that you can give to the Tribunal. You're here today, however, to enable counsel to raise with you points that they wish to clarify, perhaps to add to, and indeed to challenge. So in the course of your oral evidence here, we hope that you'll be able to concentrate upon answering the particular questions that counsel address, because in the end of the day, what we would like to do is add to the information we already have rather than simply repeat what we already know. And the first person to ask you questions will be for the Prosecution, and that is Mr. Marcussen. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kadriu.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, did you give a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in December of 2000?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And was that statement read back to you at that time?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And did you sign the statement?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: More recently, have you had a chance to read through your statement again?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, I did read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And was it discovered that in the Albanian translation there was one paragraph missing?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, one paragraph was missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And have you been given a draft translation of that paragraph that you have had a chance to read?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, I received it, I read it, and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the translation that you read and with the addition of this paragraph that was missing from the translation, is that a correct reflection of the events as you remember them?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I think, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So that if I were to ask you -- go through the whole statement and ask you about these events, you would provide the same answers as those that are included in the statement?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So I'd like to then tender this statement as P2377.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We have uploaded to the e-court system the Albanian translation of that missing paragraph, but of course it shouldn't affect the B/C/S and the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does it have a different number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: No, it is added as an attachment to the existing e-court file to avoid too many exhibits floating around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, where did you live in March of 1998?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: In March 1998 I was living at home with my family in the village of Brusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And how far is that from the village of Prekaz?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Brusnik is about 17 kilometres from Prekaze, maybe even less. 14 to 17 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You describe in your statement that on the 3rd of March you heard gun-fire and artillery fire from the direction of Prekaz, and you explain how you thought that that probably was an offensive in the area where the Jashari family was living or lived and you tried to find out what was going on. And then you say you met some people from Dubofc.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Where did you meet these people?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I was a representative of the Council of Human Rights and Freedoms, and it was our duty to be there when these things happened. So I went to Dubofc, even further than Dubofc to see what was happening in Prekaze because this village could not be seen from that village I was in. Because it's the Cicavica mountain that separates us. It's between two villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. I think those are some of the details that are already covered in the statement. What I would like to focus on with my question is you say in your statement you met some people, and I'm just wondering where did you meet the people who had come from Dubofc?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: The truth is that as soon as my left my village, it was early in the morning, a bus that was coming from Dubofc was passing through our village, and thinking to go to Vushtrri with this bus. But from the bus people got off. There were some refugees that had left these villages, and this was the first time I was informed about this. I had heard the shots before, but this is the first time I heard that the Serb police and army had surrounded some villages in Prekaze area and that they had surrounded the Jashari family. This was the first time I heard about this, but I had heard the shots before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kadriu, the question you were asked just now was a very simple question. And the question was where you spoke to these speak from Dubofc. Now, the answer was: In your own village. And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, exactly, in my own village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's four words, and we've got probably a page of a transcript of information that counsel did not ask you for. Now, can I remind you of what I said at the beginning, that you concentrate on the question and answer the specific question because we already have so much information from you. And the reason for that is, if we are going to do justice to the many cases that are raised in this indictment, we have limited time to spend on each one. That's very regrettable, but it's a fact of life, I'm afraid, that we must concentrate on the particular issues that are raised with counsel. So I invite you to do that, otherwise we will not do justice to the case. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was trying to clarify, Your Honour. I was thinking here that I'm here to testify about these events. I wanted to be more concrete in what I was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, I don't doubt your good-will in that respect, but please bear in mind what I've said to you that we, nevertheless, in spite of the wish of all the witnesses who come here to tell us a great deal more than they have already said, we do not regrettably have time for all that. We must concentrate on the things that really matter. So please help us to do that. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, you said that the people that got off the bus told you about the events. Did they tell you which forces were involved in the operation they were moving away from? You can maybe answer that with just a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What forces did they say were involved?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: According to them it was the Yugoslav army because they had artillery and tanks, but also the police, combined forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Another point of clarification about these events I'd like to move on to is what happened next in terms of your investigation. You describe in your statement how you went to Skenderaj and tried to figure out what had happened from there. And then you describe how you saw some bodies in -- in Skenderaj. I'd like you to try to explain to me the conditions in which these bodies were -- were laid out. And you say in your statement the police did not guard the place. What -- what did that indicate to you, if anything?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: It is true that three days later, after we did not hear the shots anymore, a group of the Council for Human Rights, including me, we went to the outskirts of Skenderaj. And in a construction warehouse they had put the bodies of the Jashari family, but also other victims that had been killed during this offensive. And there we made some photographs --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Just so we break this up in bits so we get it all into the record. You say "they had placed the bodies there." Who placed the bodies, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: The Serb police, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Because the bodies of the Jashari family -- well, I would say that the whole area had been surrounded before by the police, so nobody could enter that area. So they must have taken away the bodies. The bodies were also cut and so on, and they had put them in this construction warehouse. And not very far from this construction warehouse there were some houses where the police forces were, about a hundred metres from the place where the bodies were. And this was a little bit surprising for us. They must have had their own reasons why they allowed us to see those bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When you -- you explain in your statement that on other occasions you have carried out investigations into alleged killings and things like that. On those occasions, did you normally have access to bodies, if there were any?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: It's interesting and surprising. It was surprising to us that we were allowed to see the bodies, and there was a big crowd of people that came and saw the bodies. I thought that this was the beginning of the operations, so the police and the army wanted to create panic and to frighten the population. Because if you could see the bodies, it was a horrible sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were the bodies also -- were these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't want an answer to your question then, Mr. Marcussen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, you answered a question you weren't asked. The question you were asked was: Were you normally allowed to see the bodies when you made your inquiries on the council?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the answer was yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So why were you surprised on this occasion that you were allowed to see them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because before that operation we were not allowed to see the bodies. There were no exhibitions of bodies, so to say, before. So it had never happened before to be able to see the bodies -- not only us but also the other citizens. Whoever came that day was able to see the bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were pictures of the bodies also broadcasted in the media, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What media --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: -- on the public television. At that time it was Pristina Radio and Television, but we were watching the Tirana-based Pristina TV. Because when the station was called -- was closed in Pristina, their offices transferred to Tirana. So that's where we watched the operation that had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I asked you about -- I'm not sure whether this was a translation thing, but what I asked you was whether the bodies were shown in the media. And the answer came back as something with the operation, but --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We watched them on television. I remember that this was also covered in other television stations such as Sky News. But there were clips from this photograph or footage, but very short clips. I remember the Sky News.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, tell us what did the clips from Sky News show?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very brief footage of this warehouse. First they showed something about the operation against the Jashari family, and then there was this footage of people visiting the warehouse, a line of people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did that show dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only superficially. They were mostly focussed on the line of people lined up there, and there was a comment about what had happened. I don't understand English very well, but what I remember is this queue of people waiting to go and see the bodies of the Jashari family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to something else than the bodies, but related to what happened in February and March of 1998. To your knowledge, were there people fleeing the area of operations?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: From 1998 and on, from March 1998 and onwards, many people left from the area where the Serbs were carrying out these operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were you involved in -- in registering some of these people in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'd like us if we could see Exhibit P8, please, the second page of the exhibit. If we could see page 2, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If you look at the screen now, there's a document being shown. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Please just wait for my question --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: This is a register --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: My case manager quite rightly informs me that I should point out that the English version of the exhibit, what we are seeing on the screen, is actually page 4, if anybody are trying to find the English translation of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, could you just very briefly tell us what this document is.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: This document reflects the number of people who left these villages, and you have the list of villages here from the municipality of Skenderaj, but also two villages from the Vushtrri municipality. So they had left those areas and had come to our town or to villages surrounding our town. This is a list of villages, about 20, and you have the number of the refugees that left those areas. And in the end you have the total number of the people that we could register, because it was impossible to go to each and every house and take record of everybody who had left. But this reflects the situation at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And just on that exhibit, just one last short question that can probably be answered again with a yes or no. Did you provide information to the Red Cross which is included in this table?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes. The Red Cross also was carrying out its own investigations, so we exchanged information with the Red Cross and we cooperated closely with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is actually a Red Cross record, Mr. Marcussen, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It is, yeah, it has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you also describe that there was an operation that was carried out in June of 1998, a bigger operation. And you estimate that there were about 40.000 refugees coming to your municipality as a result of these operations. Did you also participate in registering these refugees that came in June?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Well, the activists of the Council for Human Rights and Freedoms, but also the Red Cross and other organisations, took part in the registration of these people. But people came mostly to the villages of our municipality. We estimated that there were about 40.000 because they were settled in Fushe Kosova, Obilic, Mitrovica, Skenderaj, so this is an estimation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, I am going to lose patience shortly. You were asked a very specific question yet again which you failed to answer. Did you personally participate - that was the question - in registering these refugees that came in June? We already know the number. We know it was a group of you that were doing it. We want to know if you personally were part of the group doing the work.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I said yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. See how easy it is? Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were the refugees given food and -- let's just keep it at food. Were the refugees given food?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course we had to give them food.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Who provided the food for the refugees?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: In addition to the families that helped them, there was also Mother Teresa organisation, it had a chapter in Vushtrri at the time; and they helped with providing food to these refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What about the authorities -- state authorities, did they provide any food for the refugees?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask you some short questions about the attack on your village on the 22nd of September of 1998. You say in your statement that you saw that in the morning -- early morning tanks were taking up position around your village. Where were you when you saw the tanks and ...

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: That morning I was at home, but when we got this information that we were surrounded and we heard the rumble of the tanks, we began to move and we wanted to take measures to leave to go somewhere, because -- especially me, who was a member of the Council for Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just describe for us very shortly -- in very short terms: The tanks you saw, how did they look? First, what were they driving on, were they driving on wheels or tracks?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: The tanks we saw were of various kinds. I saw a big tank at the cemetery of the village. Then I saw a Praga. That's what the Yugoslav army called that, a Praga. It had big barrels. Then I saw a transporter with rubber wheels, rubber tyres, and other motorised vehicles that were not far from each other. They were positioned in the direction of Cicavica where the operation would take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The tanks, what colour was the tank? I guess there was only one.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: The tanks were green, this SMB colour, olive-green-grey, while the ones who were doing the searching were the policemen on the street, while the tanks were a bit further away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, before we get to the people who entered the town, were all the different vehicles you could see and you just described, were they all the same colour, SMB?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Then you say that some people came to your village and you described them as police. Now, what kind of uniform did they have on?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I saw them earlier coming out from the house. I saw them in two houses that were not fully constructed. I saw policemen in green camouflage uniforms and blue camouflage uniforms. They had helmets on their heads, and they had anti-bullet vests. The -- these vests did not correspond to the colour of their uniforms underneath.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Okay. So --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Is it -- the people you saw who were in green uniform, were they also police do you think? That's what it says in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: The police was the one that was doing the search and forcing the people out from their houses, while the military, they were further on their positions and they were observing the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How do you know that the people who were in green uniforms belonged to the police?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: The Serb police wore three or even more than three kinds of uniforms. Sometimes they would wear blue, blue camouflage uniforms; sometimes green camouflage uniforms; and sometimes plain blue uniforms, uniforms that they used to wear in the past, before the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But -- is there anything in particular about the people in the green uniform that make you say that they were police? Could you see something written on them? Did they have insignia on that you saw, something like that?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I was able to see those insignia before, but on that particular day I couldn't. I wasn't close. But that was the impression that I had because we had seen the police forces on many occasions before and it wasn't difficult for us to identify them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The last thing about this event is, you yourself escaped and you told the young men to try to escape to the mountains. Why did you tell the men that?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I feared for the life of the young men because these operations usually ended with killings. That's why I suggested to the young men to flee and hide somewhere, in order to save their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. You then in your statement page 8, from paragraph 3, all the way through to paragraph 11, in quite some elaborate detail explain an investigation that was carried out, and you give details about people being killed and damage caused to different villages. Now, I have a very short question about that, which is: Did you yourself go to all the places that are listed in your statement?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, I went to all the places that are listed there, and I visited these places within three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Who were with you, if anybody? When you say "we" in the statements, who were the others?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: There was another colleague of mine, another activist of the Council for Human Rights and Freedoms. Sometimes we were two, sometimes we were three, depending on the possibility for movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you keep notes or other kinds of records during those days?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes. The places that I visited and the bodies that I saw, I would keep notes and forward them to the Council for Human Rights and Freedoms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you gave your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in December 2000, did you consult your notes when you were telling the Office of the Prosecutor about these events?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, because it is impossible to remember everything; that's why I consulted my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to move on to the events that happened in March, from the 27th of March, 1999, and onwards from there. And I have some specific questions that I'd like to ask you to clarify some issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But just for the information of the Court in -- on page 12 at paragraph 3 there are references to the attachment at the back of the statement. These attachments are -- you will have seen them before, these camouflage patterns. Just for reference purposes, a colour copy is found as Exhibit IC42.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Kadriu, to get back to you now. You explain in your statement that you recognised one of the policemen that came on the 1st of April. You identified him as Dragan Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How do you know him?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Every citizen in Vushtrri municipality knows Dragan Petrovic because he was known for the terror and violence that he exercised on the citizens of Vushtrri. This very same Dragan Petrovic with others would often come to the school where I worked. They were involved in the arrests and they would arrest us and take us to the police station for interrogation. So it's not only me who knew him; everybody in Vushtrri municipality knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But you have been arrested and interrogated by him, and therefore you know his name. Is that what -- was that the correct --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: When they were taking us to police stations for interrogation, he would verbally offend us and he would order his subordinates to take our personal data.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: That wasn't my question, though. Did he tell you your name -- his name, sorry. Did he tell him -- did he tell you his name either when you were arrested or when you were interrogated or how is it you know his name?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: We simply knew his name. From 1990 onwards, we always had problems with Petrovic. There were occasions -- so when the name of Petrovic and Ljubisa Simic would be seen on the end of the statements that were taken from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you describe a little further on in your statement that you saw a man named Ali Mernica and you describe how he was taken away and you think he got shot. Now, this gentleman, you explain, had been lending some of his houses to be used as schools when the school was closed down in 1991. Did you ever -- when you were giving lessons to school children, were you ever giving lessons from any of his houses?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Ali Mernica gave three or four of his beautiful houses to us to be used as Albanian schools for years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And did you have occasion to meet him personally before the events in 1999?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. You describe in your statement also when you were imprisoned you recognised different people. And I would just like you to be very -- in very short terms, just describe how you recognise these people, why you knew them? The first is Dusko Janjic, how do you know him?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: This was the second time that I was being imprisoned. After they arrested us, we were taken to Smrekovnica prison. There I recognised Janjic. I knew him from before, but he was a leader of that team that was taking our personal data before we were sent to prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And -- and where do you know his name from?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I knew his name because in 1995 and in 1997, when I was arrested for my activities in the Council for Human Rights and Freedoms and for my activities as an Albanian teacher, he had called me for interrogation to ask me questions about my activities in the Council for Human Rights and Freedom. Now I remember his full name, Dusko Janjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What about the gentleman that's referred to in your statement as Simic? How do you know him?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Simic was deputy police commander Dusko Janjic. I know Simic because he also came to our classrooms, to our parallel schools, and interrupted our lessons. I know that at one occasion he maltreated one of my colleagues. He slapped her on her face, this Ljubisa Simic, in front of the students.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In your statement you -- you didn't give a first name for Mr. Simic, but do you now remember his first name?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: It's Ljubisa Simic. It is possible that I forgot because it happens sometimes to me that I don't remember the name for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, also in the prison there were two other gentleman and they are the last ones I'm going to ask you about. Zoran Vukotic, how do you know him?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Just before 1998, Zoran Vukotic worked in the administration of the municipal court in Vushtrri. He later was mobilised as a policeman. He was a monster, a criminal, who would beat up and maltreat whoever he wanted. That's why it wasn't difficult to recognise him in the prison, because he repeated what he did elsewhere in the prison as well; he maltreated people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How have you learned his name? I understand that he was a -- according to you, he was a notorious person, but how do you know his name?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: It wasn't difficult to learn his name. You see, our municipality comprises of not that great number of inhabitants, and everybody knows everybody, so to say. As an activist of the Council for Human Rights and Freedom, I was interested to learn about him, why he was so notorious.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: He was the son of Danilo Vukotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And Sasa Manojlovic, how do you know him? And really, the basis for your knowledge of his name, please.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I didn't know Sasa Manojlovic from before. I first met him when I was sent to Smrekovnica prison. Together with Vukotic, they exercised brutal violence over the prisoners. Another colleague, a professor who was in prison with me and some other villagers from Drvar village where Sasa Manojlovic was from, they told us about him because they knew very well who he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, about the prison, how many people were in the cell that you were in?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: In the beginning, not so many, and later on we were 63 even in one cell. Everything was full, the corridors. There was no room to swing the cat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How big, approximately, was your -- the cell you were in?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: 4 by 3 or 4 by 4. I did not measure it, but that was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could we see Exhibit P46, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Is that a document that you found and gave to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I found it in the offices of the Municipal Assembly, especially in the offices of people's defence, general people's defence -- not only this document. I found other documents as well, and I have them with me here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: When did you find these documents?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date, but it was immediately after the war ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And did you yourself collect these documents?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: As a chairman of the Commission for War Crimes Investigations, I was supposed to collect this document, and we kept them in the archives of our municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The documents, when you found them, could you describe how they were located. Were they found on a desk? Found in binders? Put on shelves? Where did you pick them up?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: These documents in particular were found in a drawer in office number 9. In the beginning, we didn't think they were important, but later on they turned to be very important. Some friends who knew Serbian better than me helped me to translate these, and that's when I realised the importance of these documents and separated them from other documents that were sent to archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, this -- this document is about -- is a request for supplies to the prison in which you were detained, and there's requests for all sorts of things, flour, sugar, beans, and cattle for slaughter. Were you ever given any meat in the meals that you had in the prison? Thank you. Yes or no will be fine.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could we now move on to Exhibit P53, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: This document, is that also one that you found?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And that document is dated on the 16th of May, 1999, and it says that there are a total of 830.000 men arrested. Does that number, do you think, correspond to about the number of prisons there were -- prisoners there were in the prison where you were detained?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 830 I think is the figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What did I say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: That would have been a big prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It was, yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The prison where I was, there were about 2.000 people in there. The document that was on the monitor a minute ago shows the number of the prisoners in Smrekovnica prison, but this figure might have been in the initial stages. Later on, as I explained, as people were returned from the convoys that were heading to Albania, and brought to the prison in Smrekovnica, this number became higher and reached the figure of 2.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Related to the events in -- prior to you being detained --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'd like to -- if we could see Exhibit P2386.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, again, is this a document that you have found?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could I ask you, this first paragraph of the body of the text explains that there were -- the document is about the number of refugees in Vushtrri on the 30th of May, and it says the president of the Municipal Council is signing this document and the document says there were about 30.000 refugees at that point in time. Does that correspond to what you know about the number of refugees?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Even without having seen this document, when I gave the statement I gave you this figure, that approximately 30.000 people were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like to ask you about some more documents that you found, and then we'll get back to your investigations?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: First, could we see P1335, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, this document, is that also one of those that you found?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And it is about the -- a decision to appoint Slobodan Doknic as president of the Crisis Staff. Slobodan Doknic, do you know him?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, I know him very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: From where?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: From much earlier he was my Serbian-Croatian language teacher while I was in secondary school, and later on we were colleagues. We worked together in the Muharrem Bektashi high school in Vushtrri.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And is he the same gentleman that you talk about in your statement on page 4 in the third paragraph, who informed you that the school had been closed?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: The same person, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Then I'd like if we could see Exhibit P477 [Realtime transcript read in error "447"]. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And again, this is a document you found?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And that's a list of members appointed to the Crisis Staff in your municipality dated on the 17th of June, 1998. Among the names listed as being members of the Crisis Staff, are there any -- are there any Albanians?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: There are no Albanians on this list -- excuse me just a second. On the upper right-hand corner it says "narodna odbrana," people's defence, and beneath it it says that it's a confidential document. Just look at the upper, right corner of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you. That's reflected in the translation of the document as well. Now, I'd like us to then move on to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I made a mistake and due to the very diligent efforts of the court staff, we did get the right exhibit on the screen although there's a problem in the transcript. But at page 25, line 14, the exhibit there should be P477.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, could we see Exhibit P1334, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: This document, again, is that one of the documents you found in the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, together with the other documents that were shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And this document is a document establishing a census commission for your municipality, and it's been established by the Municipal Crisis Staff upon the 3rd of May. So that would have been the day after the convoy that you were in had come out from the northern area -- the area north of Vushtrri. What is the ethnicity --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What is the ethnicity of the people in -- in this commission?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Except for one who is Albanian, the others are Serbian or Montenegrin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, at this point I should probably ask you if you know: What is the ethnic composition of your municipality? What was it before the big movements of people, obviously, so in 1998 let's say.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Almost 100 per cent were Serbs and Montenegrins. With the -- when the autonomy of Kosovo was revoked, the Albanian workers in the administration were dismissed; only a few remained, continued to work. And among those who remained there is the name of the person who is on this list, of the Albanian on this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think that answer is to the question of the composition of the officials of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that this is completely wrongly translated. This has nothing to do with the census commission. This is some kind of recording commission. What are they going to record, it's not clear at all from this document. Because in Serbian, you don't say "popisna komisija" you say "komisija za popis stanovnistva" which is a completely different matter and this document is not serving the purpose in which the Prosecution is driving this part of the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you may be right, Mr. Lukic, but I think that's a matter for you to explore in cross-examination. Thank you for alerting us and the Prosecution to the difficulty.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I explain here, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time commissions -- census commissions were formed because the Serbian government wanted to know the exact number of people that they had expelled and the number of people who had remained there. On the 3rd of May, it was this commission -- I don't know if all the people who are listed there were its members because I couldn't see that, but this was the commission who was registering the number of the population and who were expelling the people to Albania. Of course that is not written on the document, what was the purpose of that commission, but this is what that commission was involved in doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think we'll move on to the next exhibit, that will be P8 -- sorry, P487. Could we see the second page, please, of that when it comes up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, is this also, yet again, one of the documents that you collected from the municipal office?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, it is a --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what -- carry on, what is this document, please?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: This document was found in a notebook. It's the notes of the people who were mobilised at the time. This is what we found, and we gave it to the Tribunal investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It looks to me like the -- the upper part of the document is written in Cyrillic, but then all the names are written in the Latin script. Do you have any idea why that is?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes -- I don't know. This is what we found. This is the exact document we found, and we gave it to the investigators. I didn't pay much attention to it. Sometimes they wrote things in Cyrillic, sometimes they did write them in the Latin alphabet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Before coming here today, have you had a chance to look at the names included in this list?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: When I came here to testify in the Milosevic case, I confirmed all these names and there was cross-reference with other documents as well that we found about this mobilisation of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What is the ethnicity of the people included on this list? As far as you can judge from the names.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, they're all Serbs and Montenegrins. It's been a long time that I have not seen this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to get back to a question that I asked before and I think we need to clarify the answer on that. In your municipality, how many Serbs, Albanians, and Roma were giving there, if you know approximately the relationship in percentage maybe between the different groups?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't be able to give you an exact answer, but I know that about 90 per cent or over 90 per cent were Albanians, and then the rest were Serbs and Roma and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: There was a census that was carried out in 1981. I was young at the time, but there was no other census carried out later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like to go back to your statement now and -- beginning at page 21 you describe -- you list, essentially, the victims of the convoy massacre on the 2nd of May, 1999. You have described earlier that you carried out investigations of events happening in your municipality. Did you also investigate the second convoy -- the 2nd May massacre?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I was myself in this convoy on the 2nd of May, but later on I investigated the case, because I wasn't able to see everything while I was in the convoy. So we had to investigate further on later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Of course the events in the convoy and what you experienced there is included in your statement that the Judges have accepted. So that is part of your evidence. The -- did you have somebody -- did you alone carry out the investigation or were there other people involved as well?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: We investigated together with the representatives of the investigation commission. I was head of the commission, but there were other members as well. Every fortnight we held a meeting and we discussed each case separately. We also exchanged information and reports, and we discussed all the cases. This happened every other week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And how did you collect the names included in this -- in your statement? Did you interview witnesses to the killings, for example?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, we interviewed the witnesses of this massacre, and please, Your Honours, if you need the files, I have the files of each of the witnesses, what they have said. If the Bench would like to have these files, I would make them available for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you -- you or other members of the commission who interviewed witnesses, did you take written statements from them?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes -- well, the witnesses were interviewed and we took notes, and we wrote everything. So on the left we had the witness sign the statement and then the interviewer signed on the right-hand side. I don't know if we have files for each and every one of the victims, but we have most of them. And you also must have a file from the testimony that I gave in Milosevic case with sketches of the place and names of people and so on. It must be here in the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It is indeed. We are not introducing it as part of the evidence in this case. When you gave your statement in December of 2000 to the Office of the Prosecutor and listed all these names in your statement, did you then consult the investigative file in compiling this list of names that's included on the statement?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, together with the investigators at the time; as far as I remember, yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Are you -- well, you explain in your statement also -- you explain in your statement that some of these bodies were exhumed. Do you know the location where these exhumations took place?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: It was immediately after the war. I can't remember the month, maybe July or August. There was a French team that carried out the exhumation -- not only in Studime, but also other mass graves. This case was in Studime, so the exhumation took place in Studime. But we did not have any extensive information from this team that carried out the investigation -- the exhumation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen, where is the reference to the exhumation in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think it's after the list of names. I hope I'm not mistaken -- that's obviously wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it may -- it may not matter, but it -- there is to be other evidence identifying these named victims who appear in Schedule I?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I have notified by e-mail my colleagues that I would be suggesting that we tender from the bar table the French forensic reports after the testimony of this witness -- and, sorry, yes, it actually only says that the burial -- indicated that there was a burial taking place of the victims. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you continue, can I ask one question of the witness. Was Bajram Mulaku a member of your Committee for Human Rights and Freedoms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Bajram Mulaku was either chairman or vice-chairman of the LDK, a party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not my organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'd like if we can show from Exhibit P333, page 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kadriu, this is black and white.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Can we zoom in on the top part of the photo, please, the top one. Well, that doesn't come up in the quality I'd hoped, but anyways --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you recognise this place on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes. This photograph depicts the area between Studime e Eperme and Studime E Poshtme where the killing on the 2nd of May happened. It's at the entrance of the mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In light of how the pictures looks, Your Honour, I don't want to go into it any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But this is where the mass grave was found?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, it is between the two Studimes. It is closer to Studime e Eperme.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: There is a road that can be seen on the photograph running horizontally about the middle of the photograph. Where are the -- where are the graves found, on which side of the road, closer to the viewer or further away, behind the trees?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: The graves are beyond the river. There's a river here. It's very unclear here in this photograph, but the image, the general image, from it I can see that it's beyond the river. It's the monument there and also the graves, because a monument was raised there to commemorate these victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Let's try, if we could, go to the next page, please, and see the lower photograph on that page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Can I continue with my comment? This is clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So is this the entrance to where the grave were found?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes. This is the entrance to the graves, but now there is a bridge there; so it is different now from what this photograph depicts. This photograph must have been taken immediately after the war because a bill -- a bridge has been built here and there is also a monument, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kadriu. My last question relates to --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: -- to the investigation that you were also involved in which concerned the killing of 74 people on the 22nd of May. In your statement you say that the people -- the 44 -- the 74 persons are missing. Have you, since you gave your statement, received information about what the fate of these people was?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes. When I testified then, we didn't know anything about these people. They were missing -- although we suspected that they were killed, but we did not have any proof to that. In the meantime, from Batajnica 5 bodies were returned and most of the 74 people -- the bodies of these 74 people were then buried in the cemetery for war crimes victims. But at that time, we didn't know that these victims were executed on the 22nd of May on a street which is now called the 22nd of May, and then they were sent to a mass grave in Batajnica in Belgrade. And each body had a figure on it and "Batajnica" written on it. Not all of the bodies were returned, but most of them were returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could we call up as the last exhibit for today P2393.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, this document, do you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: This document includes the name of the people who were eliminated, and the bodies of these people were returned from Batajnica. We kept record of the names when these groups of bodies were returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you prepare this list?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, together with a colleague, we both compiled the list. This is not a list of all of those that were returned. These people were killed on the 22nd of May, of course, yes, but we only wrote down names of those who were returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, that includes my questions to the witness at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So far as this event is concerned, are you going to be offering evidence of what happens at Batajnica 5?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It's my understanding that we're going to present evidence from all the Batajnica sites, although now suddenly I have doubts I must say, but that is how I understand we are going to present the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Because this is an event that's not specified in the indictment. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: That is correct --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It's not -- I'm not changing anything that I said this morning. It's simply to supplement the statement to the extent that the statement indicate that the persons are missing and the witness now knows that they are dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When was the work done on Batajnica 5?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was 2002, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you now going to deal with the matter you mentioned of tendering documents from the bar table?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If that is a convenient time or I can do it when we're finished with the witness and cross-examination is over which it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you should deal with it before cross-examination, just in case there are any issues arising.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Okay. Well, what I would seek admitted is the French forensic reports from the exhumations that took place of victims from the 2nd May massacre. The exhibits are: P331, 332, 333, and 334. There's also a summary report made by the forensic -- the French forensic team which has P206, and there the relevant pages are pages 10 to page 18. And there's a ballistic report which also concern this particular site, and that is included on page 40 of Exhibit P210. And I would seek those exhibits and parts of exhibits admitted at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What are P331 to 334?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: They are extensive forensic records of the exhumations that were taking place, documenting the unearthing of the corpses and the exhumation of the bodies to determine the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a question or a comment. As far as I understand, the OTP will, as relate -- as regards the forensic report, will have a witness who will be able to be cross-examined by the Defence. I don't know whether our cross-examination will be limited in any way if this document is now being considered. I don't know whether it should be tendered by us after our cross-examination. Technically speaking, to me it seems the same, given that we are able to cross-examine the expert of the Prosecution who will testify regarding the forensic reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That is, of course, if the Trial Chamber don't grant your motion to refuse to hear any experts. Were you suggesting that the motion doesn't apply to this expert?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps it will be best for me to suggest to postpone the decision on these exhibits, pending the resolution of our motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I hear what you say, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Marcussen, will there definitely be a witness through whom these could be tendered in any event?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I take it "definitely" meaning in case you are not granting the Defence motion, but there's a -- what we're proposing is an overview witness to -- through who we intend to present all the forensic reports of this nature, who -- yeah, who had been involved in parts of this but not all the exhumations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One of the difficulties of Mr. Visnjic's motion, of course, is that you have a number of allies on the Defence side, if in fact you're opposed to the motion. So the situation is not black and white.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Anyway, we shall reflect on your suggestion that these be admitted from the bar table, and we'll give a determination at some point in the course of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If I may, sorry, one more --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I know we are running late. I would also seek admitted something I indicated in our witness notification but didn't raise this, sorry -- bring up this morning. The witness has identified a number of policemen, and I would seek the same names appear on page 4 of Exhibit P2235. That is -- I think that has been referred to as the A response regarding alleged perpetrators and other pages of that document have been admitted in the context of testimony of other witnesses. So I would seek to tender page 4 of that particular exhibit as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, have you any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just for the record, we had the same objections we had previously regarding these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the view we've taken so far is that it's really a matter of weight in due course and that you will have an opportunity to make appropriate submissions before we decide ultimately what value these documents have.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, again we'll reflect on whether that ought to be admitted, but the decision is likely to follow that of other parts of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, we need to take a break at this stage. So you'll be shown where to wait --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Your Honour, I only have one request, because I've brought here some slides from Kosovo and you can see there the Jashari family massacre. If the Bench wants to have those slides, I can put them at your disposal as material proof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen, are you aware of the existence of these?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I am aware of the existence of these photographs, and Mr. Kadriu kindly brought these photographs at our request. I chose yesterday when I saw them that we wouldn't be trying to tender them at this late stage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Kadriu, I think everyone appreciates the effort you're making to give us as much information as you possibly can to the Trial Chamber. The issues that we have to determine, however, I doubt would be assisted by the material you're suggesting we consider. In the process that we follow here, it's normally left to the parties in the case - that's the Prosecution and the Defence - to propose the introduction of materials such as the slides you're referring to. Mr. Marcussen has indicated that having considered the position and bearing in mind the rules that apply to these proceedings, it's not necessary to do so. And we would, I think, go along from that situation. If someone from the Defence side takes a different view, then you may find you're asked questions about it. But for the moment we're grateful for the action you've taken, but we don't think that would add to the information necessary for us to decide the crucial issues in this case. The usher will show you where you can wait during the 20-minute break, if you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... please leave the courtroom before we do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll resume in 20 minutes, which will be just after 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the witness comes in, I just want to inquire how much time the Defence has with these kind of mixed witnesses, live and 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you suggest is appropriate in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know how much the other teams have -- but I'll have probably the whole session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's difficult to pigeon-hole every witness. It's easy when it's a simple crime-base witness that's presented under 92 ter essentially and is examined for only half an hour. We can deal with that fairly easily. We can deal with live witnesses fairly easily by equality with exceptions. What would you suggest in this case would be the appropriate approach?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think the Prosecution would agree with me they skipped a lot of the original statement from this witness and they focussed only on certain points. So I think we have to clarify many things that they did mention today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're not helping me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you suggest?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When we cross-examine 92 ter witnesses we have double time they have, as I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I don't think we'll need double time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you'll do your best to complete the witness within today?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And possibly earlier than the end of today. That seems to me not unreasonable in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, do you have any comment to make on that, Mr. Marcussen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We -- it is a 32-page statement, which probably exceeds some of the other ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's actually not really a problem for you. It's more of a problem for us in the overall administration of the case. The Prosecution are affected by a global figure; the Defence are not. But we're alert to that difficulty and we have to make adjustments to accommodate the exigencies of each individual witness, but hopefully there will be other occasions where it's not necessary to examine quite as long as the Rules permit and time can be recovered. If not, we will have to review the situation, but hopefully we will not need to do it. And things will sort themselves out as we go long. Mr. O'Sullivan?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The order will be: General Lukic, General Pavkovic, General Lazarevic, General Ojdanic, Mr. Milutinovic, and Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kadriu. My name is Branko Lukic. I am one of the Defence counsel of Mr. Lukic before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will first try to cover certain point -- points from your testimony today. When you were talking about exhibit P8 where it was estimated that there were about 30.000 refugees, you said the state had not provided the food for these refugees. Did you request food?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: At that time it was absurd to ask for food from the body that was expelling you from your own house. People were being expelled at gunpoints, and they not only didn't dare to come close to their offices --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. However, we saw later - because the Prosecution showed Exhibit P2386 - where aid is requested from state authorities for 30.000 people. Was food requested from the statement at that time or did the state offer it itself?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: A document that was found at the location that I mentioned earlier points out the fact that the government had that practice to show in a document as if the food has been requested or distributed, but in reality that was not the case. People were starving. They would even eat roots in order to survive. In my village during the summer of 1998 when people fled from Drenica --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So it is your testimony then that the exhibit tendered by the Prosecution today, this document, is not accurate. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No. The exhibit presented by the Prosecution is a document of the Serb government, but that document is not accurate. The document says that we should provide the prisoners and the refugees with food, but that did not happen in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke about Smrekovnica, and we'll get back to that later. Let me now ask you about your testimony today. How many people from your convoy were sent to Smrekovnica? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: There were about 30.000 people in the convoy, but when they separated us that were sent to prison from our families, at that moment I don't know how many we were. But I can say that we were a lot. The trucks were taking prisoners to this prison throughout that day. These were big trucks that were confiscated from Albanians, and they were used for our transport to the Smrekovnica prison. Later on --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If there is something you don't know, just tell me: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Excuse me, if you just allow me to explain something. Later on we learned from some prison guards that the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just a moment. As the system functions here and as Judge Bonomy explained to you, we ask you questions and you answer them. If the other side, that is the Prosecutor, believes that you need to explain something additional, they will ask you to do that. However, we don't have time for long explanations. We have your statement, we have your evidence and your transcripts, and we are trying to finish with your evidence today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Please, I'm giving the answers the way I think I should answer your question, not the way you want me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My next question, Mr. Kadriu, since you didn't tell me that you knew how many people had been sent to Smrekovnica, do you know how many men were in the convoy in which you were moving? If you say, I don't know, that's acceptable.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No, I don't know how many men were in the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know roughly what proportion of the convoy was male?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we consider the fact that there were about 30.000 people in this convoy and the document that we showed here has that figure, we could say that about 10.000 were men because the convoy also consisted of women, children, elderly, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Out of those 10.000 men, not more than 800 were sent to Smrekovnica because we saw the figure of 830 in that document.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, but within three days that number amounted to 2.000 prisoners, and there is a document that speaks of 2.000 prisoners in that prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I suppose that men were also arriving at Smrekovnica from other areas, not only from your convoy. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, there were cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of your written statement, you speak of the fact that your brother was involved in logistics in Tirana. A logistics officer. Did that involve the procurement of weapons and equipment for the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Not weapons but mainly the registration of the volunteers who were coming from other places to go and fight in Kosova, issues that were related with the recruitment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: My brother was studying in Tirana, and by the very fact that he was studying in Tirana he was a non grata person in Kosova and could not come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that you demanded a Republic of Kosovo and that you were involved in the movement for freedom of the region. Did this involve the territories -- all territories populated by Albanians, ethnic Albanians, including Greece, Macedonia, Montenegro, southern Serbia, and Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
