utterances.text: No, not Greece, but the other territories inhabited by Albanians had similar organisations. At that time we were demanding the creation of the Republic of Kosova within the framework of that Yugoslavia, and we now do not demand a republic but we demand Kosova's independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We know that. Thank you. You were also a member of the Council for Human Rights, established in 1990. Who were the people on this council, who were the members?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Are you referring to the central council or the branch where I was active? It's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your branch, which is the object of your evidence.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: In the beginning we were many members, about 70 members of the Council for the Defence of Human Rights and Freedoms. There were passive members, so to speak, and the leadership consisted of seven or eight members. Maxhuni --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the first name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- was the chairman of the branch. However, later his house was searched and due to the risk he moved to Albania and then I replaced him and became the chairman of the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we conclude that all the members of that council were ethnic Albanians?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: There were also two ethnic Turks who were members, but no representatives of other minorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You dealt with violations of human rights. Did you concentrate on the violations of human rights of certain ethnicities? For instance, did you follow just violations of the human rights of Albanians?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No. We were the body that investigated violations of human rights. But the majority -- in majority of cases the rights of the Albanians were violated. As for the Serbs, Serb government protected them. They gave them lands and properties. There was a case when a forest ranger was killed, and I filed a report to the Serbian Council for the Defence of Human Rights and Freedom. I suspected this case to be a murder, and I forwarded this information to the centre council. And I would like to emphasise again that had there been such cases, I would have investigated them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In one part of your statement you said people were being killed in Kosovo, and afterwards it was said that they were the casualties of war in Bosnia and Croatia. I don't really understand that part of your statement. Is it your testimony that somebody would die or be killed in Kosovo and the authorities would then say that the person had been actually killed in Bosnia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No, no. It must be a confusion. In this particular point I'm speaking about the young men who were serving in the JNA. When the war in Croatia and Bosnia began, the young men from Kosova did not want to come -- become criminals and killers of innocent people, and therefore they were persecuted by Pavkovic's people. These men were sent back to Kosova in coffins, and later on we would investigate these cases. This is what I meant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, just a moment, which page of the statement is this on? I remember reading it, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: English page number 4, paragraph number 5; Albanian same; B/C/S same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony today then that people who refused to serve in the army were killed?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Well, if it was for serving in the army, I myself served in 1987/1988 and completed my military service. But when the JNA was involved in the killing of civilians in Croatia, they did not want to go and serve in the JNA. They were reluctant to do so. They didn't want to go and kill innocent civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I asked you if anyone was killed because they didn't want to go to the army. I think that's what you seem to have said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Well, we would find bullet wounds on the bodies. On three bodies, for example, the body of a young man from Reznik village contained bullet wounds, so he was killed. That's why we believed that this was the case, that the officers killed the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, what you're saying is that these were Albanians serving in the JNA who refused to do what they were told and were sent back in coffins? Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. They were reluctant to participate in the war in Croatia. Officers were killing JNA -- JNA officers were killing the Albanian soldiers who were serving at that time with the JNA. There are many cases of soldiers from Kosova who -- whose bodies were returned in coffins. I want to explain here in the doctrine of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's all I need to know from you. Mr. Lukic will continue with his questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, is that the way you drew conclusions when you dealt with killings in Kosovo, whenever you would find a bullet wound or traces of injury on the body, you assumed that the persons concerned were victims of execution?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No, not in all cases. For example, there was a body who had been killed -- of a person who had been killed as a result of a shelling. It was confirmed that he was killed as a result of a shelling. Forensic experts would look at the bodies. If you allow me, Mr. Lukic, I want to explain here. The Yugoslav army existed to defend the people from attacks from outside and not to kill their own people. The soldiers from Kosova considered the civilians from Croatia as part of their own people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, we are now entering a debate which is not the purpose of my cross-examination. I did not ask you about shrapnel and similar wounds. Whenever you found indications of death by a bullet, did you draw the conclusion that it was an execution?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No, that was not always the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. We'll move on. You first heard of the KLA in 1991 you say. Do you know what the objectives of the KLA were?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. The violence, the oppression exercised by the police, the army, and other mechanisms that were at the disposal of the Yugoslav government made people flee their own homes and shelter in the mountains. We didn't want the war, but they would not leave us alone in our own houses. They would beat us up in the presence of our family members, in the presence of our mothers, sisters. My father was beaten up in the presence of my sisters; therefore, we were forced to take up arms and fight in order to defend ourselves, for self protection reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. We can then conclude that you, too, were a member of the KLA because you say "we had to take up arms and defend ourselves."

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No, personally I was not a member of the KLA. Had I been a member, I would have told you so, but I wasn't. I was a member of the Council for the Defence of Human Rights and Freedoms. It would have been an honour to be a KLA member, but I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the KLA already in 1996 launched actions in which they attacked the police forces, such as in Gornja Klina, village of Bukos, the KLA attacked a police check-point and killed two policemen from Srbica. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: There was no police station in Bukosh village; however, the police forces, sometimes accompanied by military forces, would go to villages and harass people. People, while protecting themselves, they would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please listen to the question. The question is: Do you know about the killing of two policemen at a check-point in the village of Bukos in 1996? Now, do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, but, Your Honours, there was no check-point there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on. You say "no check-point." Mr. Lukic will now obtain clarification of that from you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This killing happened in the village of Gornja Klina, which is very near your village of Bukos. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I don't think you have this right, because Klina is very far from my village. There is another Klina which is in Skenderaj municipality. If you mean Prekaze, then it is close to my village. But Bukosh, yes, it is close to my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you then aware that in Bukos in 1996 members of the KLA, headed by Adem Jashari, together with Milahim and Meho Zeka attacked this police check-point?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No. That's wrong. This did not happen in Bukosh village in 1996. I'm absolutely sure that there was no attack on Serb forces then. I think you have the wrong information. I am sure that there was no such attack in Bukosh village in 1996, as you said. But in March 1999 there was, and it wasn't an attack, it was in self-defence. Mr. Lukic, you don't have accurate information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know of an attack in Gornja Klina?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You claim it didn't happen or you don't know about it?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No, I'm just saying that I don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that Adem Jashari was one of the leaders of the KLA back in 1996?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I know that he was a KLA leader, but I don't know as of when he became a leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You know that in 1998 the KLA was so strong that it held the territory of Drenica, as you say in your statement. Can we conclude that at that moment in that area there were no Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: In 1998, with the exception of the roads that were controlled by the Serb forces, there was no Serb forces presence in the villages; but it is true that the roads, the main roads, especially, were controlled by the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether KLA members spent time in the villages within the territory they controlled?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that KLA members did not only stay in the forests and mountains, but that they also spent their time within the villages in the territory they controlled. For example, their headquarters were usually at -- or inside schools in such villages.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: They were not usually in schools, but they had their own points, I mean the KLA, but not inside the neighbourhoods or the family homes of people. If there was an empty house built by someone, they would use it, but they were not staying in people's houses. Maybe somewhere they used schools as well, but what you are saying that this is an ordinary thing, a usual thing, that they were staying in schools, I wouldn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I used this by way of example, and I didn't want to illustrate that this was a practice. Back in 1998 and 1999, were there any KLA members who did not wear uniforms, do you know of that?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Possibly, yes, because there were many people who wanted to join the KLA, and of course they did not have enough supplies to give everybody a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement of the 28th of February, 1999 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for the Chamber in English this is page 5, paragraph 5; in the Albanian, page 5, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You talk about having heard artillery fire from the direction of Cirez and Likosane. As regards that, I wanted to ask you the following: Did you hear that precisely on that day there was a KLA attack against a regular police patrol in the villages of Cirez and Likosane?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I heard the Serb artillery myself. It was early in the morning. They were shooting against Qirez and Likoshane. I did not know in the beginning that they were shelling those villages, but I could hear the noise very well. But later on when I went there, I heard that combined police and army forces had attacked these two villages. There were other villages as well that were attacked, but in these two villages people were killed. These are places that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, the question was: When did you hear about the killing of the two policemen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not hear about that. I heard later on that there was an exchange of fire, but I did not hear about the killing of the two policemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your statement says: "According to them, that's people from Cirez and Likosane, a day earlier there had been an exchange of fire between the KLA and the Serbs and two Serbian policemen had been killed in Cirez."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I might have heard later that there was an exchange of fire. But of course at that time when I gave the statement, my recollection was better. That was something I learned from other people, not something that I knew personally. However, nobody spoke about the bodies of these two policemen, it was not in the Serbian media, they did not say anything about the killing of these two policemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I hope you understand why you are being asked the question because you have signed a statement in which you said that you met people who had told you that there had been an exchange of fire between KLA and Serbs and two Serb policemen had been killed in Cirez. And all Mr. Lukic wants to know is: Did you find out the very day it happened or did you find out some other time? That's all he wants to know. It's simple. You say you can't remember and it would help if we get straight on with it. Is that correct, you now can't remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I had heard about the exchange of fire, but later on, as it says in the statement, I heard that policemen were killed. But this is not something I verified myself, it was something I was told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It does not say in the statement "later on", that's why Mr. Lukic is asking the question to find out when it was that you learned about this. And the answer I'm noting is that you don't now remember. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I don't remember exactly. It was later, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, you were not present during the conflict or the skirmish in Cirez. You haven't witnessed it?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No. I went to Cirez later, because if I had been there present in the conflict I would not be here to testify today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, we don't know that. Is it correct that you didn't see the bodies of those killed either?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes. The people who were killed, the Ahmeti family, and the Sejdiu family. This, though, happened one or two days after the battle or the exchange of fire that happened there. We also photographed the bodies of the victims, and I can show those to you, if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the people that had been killed participated in the incident on the side of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No. The Ahmeti family, none from -- no one from that family was a member of the KLA. Also, the same can be said for the Sejdiu brothers. However, there is one from Nebiu family -- a couple from the Nebiu family. They were not with the KLA, but they were armed to protect their homes. But I know from the Sejdiu family and Ahmeti family, no one was a member of the KLA. However, these Nebiu, they -- the Nebiu family, they resisted, they had arms, but I'm not sure that they were members of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All those killed during the incident were in the immediate vicinity of the skirmish. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Well, this was not a shooting range. These were villages inhabited by people, and this happened at their home. These people were told to get out of their family -- of their family home. For example, there was this Rukija woman who was shelled, and half of her skull was missing. This was a populated area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I suppose that that shell hadn't been fired from up close, but that rather it came from afar and it was directed against the positions from which fire was opened on the Serb forces. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Listen, the Serbian forces entered the village and went to Nebiu's family to search the house and they resisted. However, the woman that I mentioned, Rukija, she was killed by anti-aircraft fire, and she was on the second floor of her house and she was hit. And the upper part of her skull was missing when I saw it. I remember that body.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Here you also mention the state of those corpses. Say the corpses from the Ahmeti family, were they sent to the Pristina hospital and was any autopsy carried out?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: This is what was said at the time, and I know this because the population gathered there for their funeral and the bodies were delayed in Pristina. And the graves had been opened. We were waiting at that time for 23 people that we wanted to bury, not only the Ahmeti family. There were children amongst the victims as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You haven't answered my question. Is it correct that the bodies of the members of the Ahmeti family were sent to the Pristina hospital and that an autopsy was carried out? Do you know of that or not?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I don't know where they were, either in Pristina or elsewhere, but I know that they were returned later, and we could see that the autopsy had been carried out. We could see them -- the bodies. But however, I cannot say whether they were in Pristina or somewhere else. The bodies were returned very late in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mention your suspicions as regards the women of the Ahmeti family and that those women had been raped. In the reports you sent to the council, did you specify the names of those women?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Listen, we heard that the women were late because the men had been killed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, could you answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The question was: In your report to the council, did you put them on notice that these women may have been raped and did you specify their names?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: We did not mention the names. We only said that it is possible that this could have happened -- it's a traditional thing. It's something that has to do with a culture of the country. We wanted to send a woman to interview these women because we, as men, could not interview them. You can imagine how difficult it would be for a raped victim to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you send that woman to interview them?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No, we didn't send anyone. I asked the central committee to send a doctor, a woman doctor; however, we did not hear later whether they had sent one or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that the Jasharis were often targeted by the Serbs since they resisted in arms. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: The Jashari family was attacked earlier as well, but it did not resist at that time. It was very difficult to say whether they were resisted or not or what the extent of their resistance was because we could not hear the shots or the firing from their guns because the artillery and the shots from the police force and the army was such a rumble, and we could not get into the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the Jasharis actually applied aggressive rather than defensive tactics? They were the people or some of the people who inter alia attacked policemen and civilians?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Jashari, when he was killed, was at his home. And the question is: What were the Serb forces doing at his house? It was not the first time that his house was surrounded. Even in 1998 women of the Jashari family were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But it is also not the first time that Adem Jashari, with his brothers and cousins, attacked Serb forces and the Serbian police. Is that correct? And after that, there would always be a chase, trying to catch them.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Where do you mean exactly? Where did these attacks happen? Where did Adem Jashari and his brothers attack, because I don't have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I asked you about one such incident, and you said you had no information on that. So I will move on.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Could you please tell me: When did they attack and where? Because he was killed at his own house.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to move on. You provided your answers as regards the Gornja Klina incident. You said that you didn't know about that. When Adem Jashari was killed, there was an incident, a clash between him and other members of the KLA and the Serb forces as the opposing force. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No, that's not correct because it was the Serbs that attacked with their artillery. You cannot resist the Serb forces with tanks and artillery with only automatic rifles; that would be absurd.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that fire was opened from the Jashari house at the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: It's not correct because from the distance they were shelling the house with artillery, and then they entered there. Pavkovic can tell you better how these things are done.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, it is your testimony today that no fire was opened from the Jashari house at the Serb forces. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I don't believe they could. I was not there, but taking into account the heavy weaponry that the Serbs had, I don't think that Adem Jashari would be able to resist them. He could not face a whole army of tanks and artillery with only automatic guns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on, Mr. Kadriu. Your statement says: "We learnt that the Serb military and police forces had surrounded the house and the Jasharis had resisted. It was on the third day that the Serbs had finally managed to overcome the resistance when the Jasharis ran out of ammunition." Now, do you want to withdraw that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was not there, nobody was there. This is something I thought had happened, but later I was thinking about it and thought that Adem Jashari could not do anything against that force. Adem Jashari was killed on the first day; however, the Serb forces continued to shell the place until the third day, on the 7th, when the infantry entered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Am I wrong in thinking that you investigated this matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I investigated it later -- even recently I learned that Adem Jashari was killed on the first day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Now, you provided the statement, which I've just read to you, which talks about the Jasharis running out of ammunition. Now, we're likely to think that that refers to some form of bullet or projectile in a gun. Would we be wrong to draw the conclusion that your findings were that the Jasharis eventually ran out of ammunition and couldn't resist any longer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I thought earlier that Adem Jashari was killed on the last day, but now I have a different opinion regarding this. And people have different opinions about the event. I learned that Adem Jashari was killed on the first day and he could not have resisted the rest of the days. I thought because the Serb artillery was shelling for three days that he was killed on the last day, but this was not the case because he was killed on the first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It would be helpful if you could say things just once. You were asked at the beginning of your evidence if you had a chance to go over your statement and verify that it was accurate, and you told us after taking the solemn declaration that your statement is accurate. Are you now telling us it is not accurate any longer because of other information you have discovered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when I gave this statement, this was what I knew at the time. Even today I'm not fully convinced of this version I'm giving today. This is something I am thinking today, but, you know, there were people that say that Adem Jashari was killed on the first day; other people that think he was not killed on the first day. But we can't know exactly what happened because no one of us was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean that you cannot give us any reliable evidence about how the Jashari family died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The way how they were killed, yes, because I have the photographs and the slides here; and also, there was continuous shelling. But I don't know when Adem and when his members of the family died. Even the Serb forces don't know when Adem Jashari was killed, whether the first or the second day, because they continued to shell for three days, non-stop. The Jashari family was under shelling for three days. When Adem Jashari was killed, we don't know. The only survivor is a girl, Besarta is her name I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the course of your investigation, did you interview that little girl who, according to your words, is the only survivor of the incident?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Besarta was in a very bad way. She was very young at the time. She was not able to give information. We talked to her, but there was no official interview carried out. She was very young at the time, so it was impossible to get the information from her.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that Adem Jashari, at the very beginning of the clash, killed a special forces member, one of the people who came there to try and arrest him?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that Adem Jashari did not allow his brother Hamza to surrender, although he wanted to, but Adem threatened to kill him?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: How do you know this? Were you there inside the family --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, please answer the question. Do you know or do you not know about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't know, but this did not happen, sir, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Stop, please. You don't know. That's the end of it. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you don't know something you cannot assert that something did not take place. Either you know or you don't. As regards how I know that, well I can tell you that. This was stated by one of the OTP witnesses. Let us move on and please listen to my questions and answer. I didn't ask you --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Listen, Mr. Lukic, your comment is absurd. How could anyone know what they talked among themselves?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If he continues this way, I don't know how to control him anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, he is being controlled. Just you go on to the next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your statement at page 7 of the English version, paragraph 4; the same goes for the Albanian, you state that the Serb forces thought there were some KLA forces at Cicavica and that is why they were shelling the hills. Did the Serb forces only think there were KLA forces at Cicavica or were there some KLA forces there indeed?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: This was in 1998 or early 1999. At the time, there was no Serb [as interpreted] presence in the area, but at that time they were later shelling the villages because they wanted to frighten the population. It was Pavkovic's people who did that; I know that they shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your statement in the English page 7, paragraph 5; the same goes for the Albanian, you state --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move on to that, the transcript says: "At the time there was no Serb presence in the area." Now, is that what you said, Mr. Kadriu?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've just given an answer --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the beginning of 1999 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, just listen --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- March, April --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- to me for a moment. It's your last answer. The question was: "Did the Serb forces only think there were KLA forces at Cicavica or were there some KLA forces there indeed?" And your answer was, according to the transcript: "This was in 1998 or early 1999. At the time, there were no Serb presence in the area."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant KLA forces. That's a mistake. I meant KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That clarifies it. That makes sense now. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also state at page 7, paragraph 5, that the war between Serbs and the KLA began in Drenica around June, 1998. This is precisely the area held by the KLA at the time. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, as far as Drenica is concerned, but not the other part of Cicavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And due to the fighting between the KLA and Serb forces, already at that time around 40.000 people moved out from Vucitrn and Mitrovica municipalities. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Can you please repeat your question; it doesn't seem complete to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that due to the conflict between the KLA and Serb forces, around 40.000 people moved out from Vucitrn and Mitrovica municipalities -- sorry, Srbica and Vucitrn?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No. We can't say that. There was fighting between the KLA and Serb forces, but the Serb forces were exercising oppression over the civilian population, Mr. Lukic. The KLA were guerilla units, and they were moving. They were not fighting all the time on a front line, but it is true that the Serb forces exercised pressure over the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that this conflict spread to include Sajice, Dobovac, Galice, Bitici, Osljane, Okrastica, Zilivoda villages which in fact constitutes an entire half or the eastern part of the Vucitrn municipality? Sorry, sorry, the west part, the entire west part of Vucitrn municipality.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, the western part. Later on in that part, it is true that here and there KLA units were beginning to be formed, established.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After this offensive and the clashes between the KLA and Serb forces, people returned to their homes. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Which offensive are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes. This happened between 22nd and 24th of September. The population began to return in some parts, not in all villages. For example, in my village people came back, but in other areas they couldn't go back to their homes because they had their homes burnt.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your statement on page 8, in English paragraph 4, and the same goes for the Albanian version, you say that you went to Galica in Vucitrn municipality and found 11 bodies there. You did not see how those people had died. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: That's not correct. Not in Galice but in Cicavica mountains. We found them at Cicavica mountains but buried them in Galice. These young men were from Galice and there were children among the victims as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There were three 16-year-olds among the victims; we can see that.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: 16-year-olds, 17-year-olds, 22-year-olds, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A person 20 years old, not even 16, in a state of war is not a child; they can carry weapons.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No, these were civilians. The Serb logic was that just because they were Albanians, they were all soldiers. So whoever had --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. But, please, could you answer my question. You did not see how those people had died, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No, I only saw the bodies --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Nobody in fact saw how those people had died.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No, they didn't say, but they could hear the screams. Sabit Mehmeti and two or three other persons who were with him could hear the screams while these victims were being massacred. They were hiding there nearby in the mountains and could hear the screams, while for -- as far as the burial of these bodies is concerned, I, together with many other villagers, buried these bodies in Galice.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You personally don't know whether those people were armed or not. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I am sure they were not armed. Some of these 16-year-olds were my pupils -- not my pupils, but they were pupils in the school where I was teaching. They were civilians who had fled the Serb terror, the Serb violence, and sheltered in the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: They were from Galice village; that's not --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's not your village. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: That's correct. But it still is in my municipality and not very far from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you claim with any certainty today that those people were not armed at that time when they were killed, when they died; and if you can, then on what basis?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I'm fully convinced that not only these 14 persons that we buried in Galice, but many others as well who were killed on that day were not armed. I'm fully convinced about this because I knew some of the victims. For example, a father and two sons were killed, a 16-year-old son and a 7-year-old son. Here are their names Gani Ademi, Fatmir Ademi, one of them was 16-year-old, the other 7-years-old. Please, these are pupils. Why, Mr. Lukic, are you insisting this much about this case when I know that you yourself believe that that is not the case. These were civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic doesn't believe anything as far as this case is concerned, Mr. Kadriu; he represents parties who may believe certain things, but he is not a person who can be accused of believing things so far as this Tribunal is concerned. This is a place of which it is suitable for us to interrupt. We'll resume for one-half of an hour and we'll resume at 10 minutes to one. You'll again be shown, Mr. Kadriu, where to wait.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, the age of the second son is 17, not 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, we are trying to finish with your evidence today, but I'm afraid that if we continue, as we have been doing so far, we won't succeed. That's why I would like to try to ask you to try to focus and to give me brief, precise answers so we can finalise your testimony today. To save time, I'll skip a couple of pages from your statement and go to page 13, paragraph 3 of the English version, which is page 12, last paragraph, in Albanian. And there you say, describing the situation in your town, you heard the police yelling and telling people to go to the cemetery. You also say that at the cemetery, which the civilians were leaving, there was no police. You found there a bus of a tour company Hajra Tours and those buses were driving people out of Vucitrn. The company drivers were telling people that they should go out of Vucitrn and into Macedonia. You did not listen to the advice given by the bus drivers and you did not go to Macedonia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: It is true that there was no police at the cemetery. The police was emptying the town and making the people move in the direction of the cemetery. I think there were three buses of Hajra Tours company, and the drivers told us that they were forced by the police to take these people out of the town to Macedonia. Some people got on the bus, but there was not enough space for everyone. So there were people on foot who was going -- who were going in the direction of Macedonia. I didn't go to Macedonia; I went to Shala e Bajgores area. I waited for the evening to come in order to proceed, and that's how I got to some villages that are in Shala e Bajgores area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're definitely not going to finish today if you continue this way.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I came to testify here, and you cannot answer your questions by simply yes or no. Some questions do need explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So your answer to my question is that you didn't take the advice of the bus drivers who told you to go to Macedonia; instead, you went elsewhere. Where did your family go?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: My family got on the bus. My mother, after 2 or 3 kilometres, noticed that I was not joining them, and she made the other members of the family get off the bus. So they got off the bus and stayed in these outskirts near the cemetery, and they stayed at the house of some uncles until the war ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So they didn't take the advice of the drivers either to go to Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes. They did take the advice, but since I did not join them, my mother made my family get off the bus. My parents, my sister, they got off the bus and did not proceed the journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Nobody prevented you from going to Gornja Sudimlja. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: It was a risk that I took. It was dangerous to cross the main road, but we took that risk and reached that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You went to Gornja Sudimlja, which at that time was a stronghold of the KLA. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: From lower Studime to upper Studime that's how the road goes, and that's where we went. It was a KLA area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You went to the house of the KLA commander Musa Terbunja. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, I wanted to spend the night there, but the house of Musat Terbunja who used to be my colleague, he was a professor, it was full of people. And at this point I do not remember whether I asked for food and proceeded to Cecilia. But I think I asked Musa's mother to give us food and proceeded to Cecilia. I remember that his house was full of refugees who had fled the villages nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that it is important for these proceedings whether you were offered food or you asked for food, or you're just answering in the way you're answering to avoid the questions that are crucial to this trial, in the hope that we will be forced to curtail your examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know what meaning it has to you, but for me food was important --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, well, please stop, Mr. Kadriu. Yes, Mr. Marcussen, what were you going to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The witness has answered and let's move on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, the witness hasn't answered. Mr. Lukic's point was perfectly justified. Please confine your answers to the questions you're asked, Mr. Kadriu. We've got lots of information already in your statement. You do not need to go over it all again. You only need to deal with the particular points that are raised by the examiner. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In these villages, Gornja Sudimlja and Cecilia, there were quite a number of KLA members and also quite a number of civilians. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: That's correct. I don't know how many soldiers there were, but there were soldiers, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This area at the time was not controlled by Serb forces; it was controlled, instead, by the KLA. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: There were some parts of this area that were controlled by Serb forces. I think that up to Samadrexha the Serb forces were there, but in the other part they weren't present there, for example, in Studime and Cecilia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The KLA continued to put up strong resistance up to April 1999, as you say in your statement, in the English version page 4, paragraph 1. When that attack began that lasted all the way until end April 1999 -- sorry, when did that attack begin? How long did the KLA continue to put up resistance in that area?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: The mountainous area of Shala e Bajgores was overpopulated with Albanians. I don't know the exact number of days, how long the KLA continued to put up resistance, but the Serb forces were advancing at all times and from all directions, from Mitrovica, Podujeva and Srbica. They had taken important positions in these villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that the resistance lasted at least from end March -- at least until end March 1999?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No. There was resistance from a guerilla point of view until the end of May. There were certain army cells that put up resistance here and there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the KLA informed the people that they could no longer resist Serb forces and suggested to the civilian population that they should leave the area they had until then controlled?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the people take these instructions, did they obey these instructions of the KLA and start to leave the area?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: The army told the people: We can no longer protect you, so go in the direction of town. But when we left, we were forced to do so because of the artillery forces. Shells were falling in Sllakofc, and there was no place where you could stay, and also the infantry forces were advancing. Usually they would shell the area first with their artillery forces, and then the infantry would enter. Therefore, we were left with no other way out but to go in the direction of Vushtrri.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the moment when you left the area, you had no contact with Serb forces whatsoever; instead, you were just obeying the instructions of the KLA. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No. Nobody would have followed the KLA instructions if the Serb shells didn't fall, but it is the shells that made every family, every tractor, every person on foot to leave. If we were left in peace there, we wouldn't have followed those instructions; there was no reason to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that the KLA issued such and similar instructions to the inhabitants of other areas as well?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you arrived at Cecilia which is on page 14, paragraph 5 of your statement, you saw just several soldiers of the KLA. A day earlier it had been a stronghold of the KLA. So you were not in Cecilia when the soldiers left it for Vucitrn. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: When the civilians left for Vucitrn.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Kosova Liberation Army was withdrawing towards a road that was leading to Dumnica. I learned later that they withdrew to Dumnica while the population continued in the direction of the town. These are two opposite roads, even if you see it on the map, you will see that they go to opposite directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did all members of the KLA go to Dumnica, or is it the case that some of them mingled with the civilian population after discarding their uniforms and weapons?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I didn't see them discarding their uniforms. Nobody discarded their uniforms. I know that they collected their wounded and that they set off in the direction of Dumnica area. This was what happened. Nobody took out their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it the case that the KLA members then moved together with a convoy of civilians, still wearing their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No. This did not happen. Don't forget, Mr. Lukic, that we, civilians, continued our journey, but there was another point of the KLA in Studime; Cecilia and Studime are two different villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony today that all the units from Cecilia set to breakout towards Dumnica?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many of them got killed in this attempted breakout?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. What attempted breakout?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In order to breakout from the encirclement of the Serb forces, we can assume that at some point they had to come into contact with those forces and that fighting ensued. Do you know if such fighting occurred and how many soldiers got killed in this fighting?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I don't know about this. I don't know. I only know that on the 12th of May we buried a soldier who was the son of the brother of one of my friends. We were there in the funeral --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can read that in your statement. It's Fadil's nephew, Beqiri, a soldier of the KLA. What I want to know is: What happened to KLA members from Gornja Sudimlja which you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: These were also going towards Dumnica. We were going towards Vushtrri, and they were going towards Dumnica. I learned later that all of them went to Dumnica. The last soldiers that were there were two soldiers who did not allow the convoy to take a turn because they knew that the Serbian forces could see us if we took that turn. So they were there to warn us not to take that turn. We could not protect ourselves. That was a machine-gun up in the hill --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can read all that in your stadium. All I wanted to know was about these members of the KLA. So it is your testimony that nobody -- no members from the KLA from Gornja Sudimlja joined this convoy of civilians? Are you sure or maybe you don't know whether somebody joined.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I am sure that they were not there, the KLA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you knew all the soldiers of the KLA. So that you know for a fact that none of them was in the convoy of civilians.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No soldier of the KLA was dare to join the convoy because they would be executed. They knew that; that's why they went in a direction of a place where they would be safer. Why would they join the convoy? Everybody knew that we would have problems with the Serb forces. We didn't know that they would kill us, but we knew that they would stop us and ask information of us. So it was impossible for the KLA soldiers to join the convoy; that would be absurd.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You spoke after that that the police led the operation of checking the identities of people in the convoy when you were gathered all in one place, and you said that they listed men, women, and children. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Not in the convoy, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next day when you --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then we saw that a certain number of people were separated from your convoy, and they were taken to a prison in Smrekovnica. Is it the case that the men who interrogated you in the prison in Smrekovnica wore civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you questioned about your possible membership in the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No. When they took notes, we were in the convoy. So when they took our personal details, that was it. They did not ask us whether you were here or there. Janjic from the security forces, he knew me and he asked something like: Where you were, why were you there? And he, as I said, recognised me and asked other people to take my personal details.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you about the prison in Smrekovnica. Were you questioned?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, some days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The people who interrogated you, were they wearing civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: There were two people in uniforms there, while the others were in civilian clothes and there was a secretary, a woman, who was taking notes, but there were two in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they interrogate you as regards your membership with the KLA when you were being interrogated in Smrekovnica?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes. And can I explain something here because you're asking this question? Would you be so kind as to listen to the explanation I have? I was captured at Studime -- between the two Studimes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you told them that you were in fact from the area of Cicavica; that's all in your statement. You mentioned the incident with Ali Mernica, and you said that you don't know whether the uniforms that the armed men were wearing were monochrome or multi-coloured or camouflage --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the reference in the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see any patches or insignia on their uniform?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes. This was on the 3rd of May. In addition to the policemen in camouflage uniforms, there were some other policemen wearing the older uniforms and they had some marks here in different colours. Insignia, it was red and blue and another colour -- I'm not sure about the colours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you talk about the murders of the people in the convoy which took place according to your statement on the 2nd of May, 1999 - and later on we have the list of all those killed - from all that we can conclude that you didn't see who killed those people and how.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: The Serb police and army forces killed them, the one that -- the ones that intervened. Who else could have killed them? We were surrounded by Serbian forces, both army and police. They later on passed there with their own convoy, and they had their own vehicles, armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was asking you whether you saw it.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I saw the police forces and the army forces that passed through the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see the murders?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I did not see the killings. I saw one person being killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We know that from your statement. But in that portion of the statement, you also state that you don't know who it was because it was dark and you couldn't see who it was or what type of uniform they wore.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But the military and police forces were there. Who else could have done that? It was also those forces that also took us to the prison in Smrekovnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We may conclude that all the murders you mentioned in your statement as well as the names of the people who were killed, we may conclude that you saw none of that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I was in the Studime massacre. I heard the shots, as I told you, because the convoy was divided in two parts. And the shots were heard all the way to Vushtrri. I saw with my own eyes when a boy was killed in front of us, but later when we did the investigation, we met the witnesses, the eye-witnesses that also knew the killers. And I have files and plenty of documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, law of diminishing returns is taking over. You're asking questions to which the answer is obvious from the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm finishing, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to ask you this: The photographs which you took, according to your words, refer to the Ahmeti and Jashari family, you took those photographs only after the autopsy was carried out on those bodies. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more question. At the Milosevic trial at page 1626 [sic] you say --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction 1676.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "Many people decided to go to Vucitrn and Macedonia to get away from the combat area for the war." Do you still stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: We had to go somewhere because it was impossible to stay there when the Serbian forces entered because they violated people, maltreated people in front of their own families. So we had to go somewhere, either to Albania or Macedonia. It was the Serbs that were telling us where to go. It was the police forces that were telling us: Leave this place. Go wherever you want, but don't stay here. And some of them ordered us to go to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is what you stated in Milosevic correct or not?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that your family stayed in Vucitrn up until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, after they were ill-treated. Our family was ill-treated. We were sent to that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions for you, but I have no doubt that some of my learned friends will.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Marcussen, are the photographs part of the process?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: No. There are some things about the transcript that we may need to clarify, but we can do it at a time convenient. I don't want to interrupt the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Kadriu. I have a few questions for you. Do you know until what year did Albanian conscripts leave for the JNA to do their military service?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Do you mean the conscripts?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, for the regular military service.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I think up to the 1990s, maybe 1987, 1989, 1988 -- up to 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today during the examination-in-chief that was conducted by Mr. Lukic [sic] at page 48 -- or maybe it was the cross-examination, you said that Pavkovic's men -- well, you commented on their behaviour towards those conscripts; therefore, you meant the period up to 1988 or 1989. Was that a metaphor? I don't want to put too leading a question.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Pavkovic was an officer at that time as well, and I think he was high up in the military hierarchy. Sainovic as well. If Milutinovic had signed Rambouillet, the situation would not be the one it is today, but they didn't want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Sir, it is rather late in the day, and I'd kindly ask you to focus. You testified before this Tribunal in the Milosevic case on the 6th, 7th, and 8th of March, 2000 [as interpreted]. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 2002.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember the dates, I just remember the year, 2002, not the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'll try to refresh your recollection as regards part of your testimony. This is the transcript for the 8th of March, 2002.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Thank you for reminding me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You were cross-examined then by Mr. Milosevic as well as the amicus curiae. At page 1776 and 1777, lines 1 through 6, you said the following -- Mr. Milosevic asked you: "Do you know how many terrorist attacks were carried out in Kosovo-Metohija since 1991 up until June 1999?" You answered: "I don't. I don't know of such attacks because the state apparatus was in your hands and you used it for certain purposes."

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: There was a hierarchy, there was a pyramid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Sir, we have no time. Yes or no, did you say that?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, Milosevic was the main one, and then Sainovic, Milutinovic, and the others. And I think Sainovic had a very important role. I am trying to answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, Mr. Kadriu, what you're saying is no answer to the question. Please listen to the question and answer the questions you're being asked. You're not being asked your opinion about the guilt of the accused here; that's a matter for us to deal with. You're being asked a specific knowledge about KLA attacks. That's all. Now, confine your answers to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Your Honour, the counsel is asking questions and making comments. If he is making comments, then let him make comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He made no comment. Tell me what comment he made.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He is not allowing me to explain and to give my answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You are not being asked to explain; you're being asked specific questions which you must listen to and you must answer. You're doing no good to this process by behaving the way you've been behaving in answer to questions in cross-examination. Now, Mr. Aleksic, if you feel the need to ask these questions about: Did you say that, then please ask them. But why should we doubt that he said it if it's in the transcript and why do you need to ask him? Then you end up with an explanation that the witness wants to give because he thinks he's being expected to say more.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, the reasons for asking such questions and for quoting portions of the transcript is because our OTP learned friends have not sought to tender the Milosevic transcript as part of their exhibits --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, would you like to tender it then? Well, you'll get your chance in due course. You don't need to ask the witness. You can tender it as part of your case in due course, but if there's a question that you need to put to this witness which otherwise you can't deal with in some other way, please ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will move on to that topic which have nothing to do with the statement and the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, after the events in 1999, were you politically active in 2000 and 2001?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, for a year I was active.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In 2000 and 2001, were you a member to any political party?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which party?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I was a member of the Alliance for the Future of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: The Alliance for the Future of Kosovo. During the time of your membership with that organisation, were you a member of the municipal board, or rather, that party's leader for the municipality of Vucitrn and you were their candidate at municipal elections held on the 28th of October, 2000?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: In the beginning, I was not chairman, somebody else was; later on, I became chairman and I was a candidate in the elections, yes. How is this related, though? I have come here to testify about war crimes, not about things after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Would you tell me who is the president of that party, Mr. Kadriu.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I don't know because now I'm not a member. It's been three years. I'm not a member anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Kadriu, I will paraphrase or reformulate the question. Who was the president back in 2000 and 2001? What is the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Your Honour, do I have to answer these questions about after -- the period after the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what is your objection to answering them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because he's tendentious in his question. This is a provoking question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why is it provoking to be asked the name of a chairman of a party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a provocation because I have come here to testify about the years of the war and not after the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can be asked any question that is relevant to the issues that we have to decide, and one of the issues we may have to decide relates to how trustworthy a person's evidence may be. And if that person has particular interests, then that might affect our assessment of the trustworthiness of his evidence. And therefore, counsel are entitled to explore other matters relating to the interest of witnesses in the affairs of Kosovo. Now, I don't know what is going to be said in due course at the end of this case based upon the answer to the question you're now being asked. But unless there is some reason related to the security of the person involved or there is some other issue affecting your safety or other members of the public, then you're bound to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think this is in the interest of the case because my personal issue after the war, it's a different thing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, that's not for you to determine. Would you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what was the question again? If the -- Your Honours, you think this is important, I will give the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you trying to tell me now that you don't remember this question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't remember the question. Could the question be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question that you feel so strongly about refusing to answer, you don't actually remember the question now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember the exact wording of the question. If possible, could the counsel repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, ask it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, you said that in 2000 and 2001 you were a member of the Alliance for the Future of Kosovo and, for a while, their municipal board president. Can you tell the Court what was the then-president of the Alliance for the Future of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: In the beginning when the party was formed, the president of the party was Ramush Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kadriu, my name is Djuro Cepic, one of the counsel for Mr. Lazarevic. I have a few questions for you. First of all, let us address the convoy and the events of the 2nd and 3rd of May, 1999. At page 78, lines 11 and 12, you said that you saw the MUP and VJ forces going through the convoy, and you gave a very detailed description and statement back in 2000. In that statement, starting from page 16, you describe in detail all the events concerning the convoy and your detention at the Smrekovnica prison. Not in a single place in the statement did you mention the Army of Yugoslavia as regards the convoy. Where did that come from today? Did anyone suggest to you what you should say here today?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I mentioned it or not in my statement; however, nobody suggested anything to me. I'm certain that artillery and motorised forces and other combined forces showed clearly that they were military forces. The police did not have tanks or anti-aircraft artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir, but you didn't mention that anywhere in your statement, and yet you accepted the statement as given by you and you signed it. The events took place in 1999; the statement was given in 2000. Please let me finish. The statement was given in 2000, and after that, you testified in the Milosevic case. And the details you've described today were never mentioned up until this day. This is what the question is all about, Mr. Kadriu.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: In my statement I always said "Serb forces." I didn't want to make any distinction between them because they were combined and they went everywhere together; that's why I used the term "Serb forces."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why do you say, Mr. Cepic, that what is in page 16 doesn't refer to the army?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, page 16, paragraph 1, reads that certain Serb forces approach. In paragraph 2 on the same page --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Please allow me, Mr. Kadriu.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 2 he says he couldn't distinguish or clearly make out the Serb uniforms of the people who were at the head of the convoy. And then further on, "as I've explained, it was quite dark and I couldn't make out the uniform they wore." He continues then with his explanation of being brought to the hangar. And the next day, page 17, paragraph 1, he says the entire area was surrounded by the Serbs in blue camouflage uniforms. There is never any mention of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic could just as easily say that in the earlier paragraphs of the page there is no reference to the police.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I used is "Serb forces," this term.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, but with your leave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Carry on -- hold on. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I do believe there is mention of military vehicles, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Page 16 in the second paragraph. "We could hear the sound of tractors and heavy military vehicles."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. You have the witness's answer that his reference was to Serb forces at the time. Now, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can we conclude, therefore, that that night you couldn't see or you couldn't make out the uniforms as you stated in your statement. Isn't that correct? This is the 2nd of May I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: That's correct. It wasn't easy to tell between uniforms because it was dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: However, when we got to the town, the Serb forces were moving on with the armoured vehicles. I thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kadriu, but I didn't ask you about that. I was asking about something else. It seems you have provided clear answers as regards that, but let us now go back to Prekaz and the events of the 3rd of March, 1999, and the arrest -- sorry, 1998, and the arrest of Adem Jashari. Today on several occasions we heard from you that artillery was used and Adem Jashari's house was targeted by that artillery for three days. Not only is it illogical, Mr. Kadriu, but I also wanted to put to you that the army and artillery were not involved in those incidents at all as regards the arrest of Adem Jashari. What would be your comment to that? What I'm stating here is an assertion.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: This is what you say, sir, but I'll tell you something. My village from the Jashari village --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Sir, just a second. This is what was said by OTP witnesses; these are not my words. Are you from the village of Prekaz? Are you from Prekaz, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No, I'm not from Prekaze village, and I've stated that in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Were you in Prekaz at that day?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No, nobody could go into Prekaze village at that day. Excuse me, I want to explain here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, a moment. You've asked a question, and then you've prevented the witness from answering that question and that needs to be rectified. Mr. Marcussen, what --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well, that was a point and I think we have been through that earlier today, the same point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kadriu, you have been asked to comment and you shall be allowed to comment on the assertion that's been made based on what other witnesses have said that there was no heavy weaponry involved in the attack on Jashari's house. What is your comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can assert to you that there were heavy weaponry there. You could hear the rumble of artillery vehicles from in my house. You could hear the sound of anti-aircraft weapons for three days in a row, and I am fully responsible for these things that I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cepic, we're going to have to continue this tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you able to estimate how long in total further Defence cross-examination will take tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you allow me, I have questions just for 15 minutes, roughly 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe I will be done by the end of the first session. In the meantime we contacted the OTP, and I believe we will finish the second -- the other witness as well; therefore, we'll have nothing left. We should be able to complete the following witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kadriu, your evidence will have to continue tomorrow. We can't continue further today because of another case occupying this court in the afternoon. So you have to be back here to continue your evidence at 9.00 tomorrow morning. Meanwhile, it's vital that you have no discussion about your evidence with anyone. Now, that means discussion either about the evidence you've given or the evidence you may yet give tomorrow. You can talk about anything you want to anyone else that you wish, but you must not with anyone discuss any part of your evidence. So please leave the courtroom now, and we'll see you again at 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Court will now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 19th day of October, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
